sections.history: Venjamakoodal stands on the east bank of the Kudaganaru river in the Kongu country, some sixteen kilometres south-west of Karur on the road towards Aravakurichi. It is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, and local tradition reckons it the fifth of the Kongu Nadu temples praised in the Tevaram, where Sundarar sang a decad in honour of the Lord of this place. The name is explained as the meeting place, the koodal, of Venjan, a hunter chieftain said to have ruled this land and to have worshipped Shiva here. The temple is described as more than a thousand years old, though its present buildings took shape over later centuries and the founding patrons are not firmly recorded. The Lord is revered as a self-manifested linga, and worship has continued here without a break.
sections.architecture: A five-tiered rajagopuram marks the entrance, and both the sanctum of Shiva and the shrine of the goddess face east. The linga in the sanctum is about five feet tall and is spoken of as wearing a serpent ornament, while the image of the goddess stands some two and a half feet high. Around the inner courtyard are shrines to the Panchalingams, to Bhairava, to the sixty-three Nayanmar saints and to other deities. The scale is modest and the setting rural, and the charm of the place is its quiet.
sections.legends: The tradition most dear to Venjamakoodal is that here the Lord gave Sundarar gold. In the local telling, Shiva came in disguise, as an aged householder or, in another version, as an old priest, and pledged His own sons Vinayaka and Murugan to an old woman, who was the goddess herself, in exchange for gold, which He then placed in the hands of His devotee. Another memory is of the hunter king Venjan, who worshipped the Lord here and gave the place its name, and of Indra, who is said to have come to this shrine seeking release from a sin. The accounts differ in the telling, and are best held as cherished tradition rather than recorded history.
sections.festivals: The year's great festival is the ten-day Masi Brahmotsavam in February and March. Margazhi Tiruvadhirai, in December and January, honours the Lord as Nataraja, and Aipasi Annabhishekam in October and November bathes the linga in offerings of cooked rice. Tirukarthikai in November and December is kept with lamps, and Maha Shivaratri falls in February or March. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Venjamakoodal asks for a slow, quiet morning. Come beneath the five-tiered gopuram, walk the inner courtyard past the shrines of the Panchalingams and the Nayanmars, and stand before the self-manifested linga of Vigirthanatheswarar before turning to the goddess in her east-facing shrine. If you know the story of the gold, hold it in mind as you pray, for it is a place where devotees ask the Lord for what they truly need. The river nearby and the farmland beyond give the visit a country calm, far from the bustle of Karur.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Venjamakoodal is a village about 16 km south-west of Karur on the road towards Aravakurichi, on the east bank of the Kudaganaru. Karur, which has the nearest major railway station, is the usual base; buses run towards Aravakurichi, and an auto or taxi from Karur completes the way. The airports at Tiruchirappalli and Coimbatore are the nearest major ones, each a few hours by road. As this is a small village shrine, confirm the exact route and timings locally.
